paras: The lynching of John Turner was the hanging of a Black man by a mob at Warren, Arkansas, shortly after midnight on the night of April 5-6, 1903. He had been jailed on a charge of assaulting a white woman, Mrs. W. H. Neely, and was taken from the county jail and hanged in front of the court house. A coroner's inquest attributed the killing to unknown parties, and Black newspapers later entered the case in their lists of the year's lynchings.

According to the reports, Mrs. Neely, a white woman of about thirty, lived about seven miles west of Warren. The Little Rock wire said an "attempted assault" on her took place on Friday, April 3, and that the accused man was arrested the next day and taken before her, and she "positively identified him." The Pine Bluff Daily Graphic's special from Warren instead said that he had "committed an assault" in which she was "considerably injured," and that officers caught him after he fled and put him in jail at Warren to await trial.

Shortly after midnight on Sunday night, a mob broke into the county jail and took the prisoner out. The Graphic gave the time as 1:15 o'clock and said the mob "was composed of white people" who worked "quietly, but in a very determined manner." The mob hanged him from a limb in front of the court house, a place where, the wire noted, "several other negroes had been lynched at different times in the history of this town." No shot was fired, and residents next door reportedly did not hear the disturbance. According to the wire, Turner "denied his guilt to the last."

The coroner cut down the body and held an inquest, which found that the lynching was "at the hands of unknown parties." No report of arrests, a grand jury inquiry or prosecutions appears in the coverage.

The Pine Bluff Daily Graphic printed the first account on April 6 under the headline "A Lynching at Warren," calling the victim John Tanner, seventeen, and "the brute." Its special treated the assault as fact, and the Newport Daily Independent reprinted it on April 8 as "Speedy Vengeance Meted Assaulter." Outside Arkansas, a Little Rock wire naming him John Turner ran on April 7 in papers from Texas to Utah under headlines such as "Negro Lynched" and "Colored Man Lynched," and the Colfax Gazette repeated it in its weekly digest on April 10. These wire versions framed the charge as an attempt and recorded both the identification and his denial of guilt.

No original report by a Black newspaper was found. In May the Rising Son reprinted a Buffalo Express paragraph that treated the choice of a spot "in front of the jail or courthouse" as an expression of mobs' "contempt for law" and cited the Warren lynching as an example. The Seattle Republican and the Sedalia Times listed "John Turner" among the year's lynchings, and the Chicago Broad Ax's year-end chronology recorded him at Warren for "attempted assault on white woman."

The local Graphic special named the victim John Tanner, while the wire and every Black list named him John Turner; the accounts otherwise describe the same man, accuser, place and night. The two versions also differ on the charge, the Graphic describing a completed assault with injury and the wire an attempted one.

accounts.label: Pine Bluff Graphic special from Warren
accounts.gist: John Tanner, 17, 'committed an assault' that injured Mrs. Neely, fled, was caught by officers and jailed; a quiet, determined mob of white people hanged him at 1:15.

accounts.label: Little Rock wire
accounts.gist: John Turner, arrested for an attempted assault and identified by Mrs. Neely, was taken from the jail after midnight and hanged in front of the court house, denying guilt to the last; the inquest blamed unknown parties.

accounts.label: Black-press lynching lists
accounts.gist: Record 'John Turner' lynched at Warren, Ark., on April 6 for assault or attempted assault on a white woman.

framing.detail: The Graphic stated the assault as fact, called the accused 'the brute' and his act 'the outrage', and described the mob as quiet but 'determined' (headline 'A Lynching at Warren'); the Newport reprint headed it 'Speedy Vengeance Meted Assaulter'.
Out-of-state papers ran the Little Rock wire under heads like 'Negro Lynched' and 'Colored Man Lynched', noting the identification and that Turner denied his guilt.
The Rising Son reprinted a comment that lynchers choose spots before the jail or courthouse to show 'contempt for law', citing Warren; other Black papers entered the case in lynching tallies.

conflicts.note: Same man, same place, same night, same accuser; one is likely a misspelling. The wire spelling was carried by every other paper and the Black lists; the Graphic's was the local special.
The Graphic states the act as completed; the wire calls it an attempt.
